links.note: Asks the main message the writer intends; the answer is perseverance and self-belief in achieving one's dream. Not 28246 (what the dream IS) but how a dream is made to come true.

What the story teaches about courage and determination - Jahnavi following the River's advice and entering the classroom. This is the 'how could she make it come true' question, not the dream itself (28246).
How the story shows support from others matters in achieving one's dreams: the River's advice plus the teacher's home visit. Sits on making the dream come true, not on 28245 the family.

Colour of the lizard. The green lizard, the kingfisher and the parrots are the creatures Jahnavi rules out as the source of the voice, in the passage where the River first speaks. Not 28244 (the River's own voice and opinions).
Asks what visual image 'an arrow of blue in the sunlight' creates for the kingfisher - a descriptive/sensory-word question about how we see something, not a plot question.
Which creature's wings are described as an 'arrow of blue'; the item is anchored on the descriptive phrase itself, so it tests the sensory description rather than 28244 the River.
The earthen floor of the classroom - a detail of the school Jahnavi creeps into, the chapter's only school concept. Not 28243 (Jahnavi herself).
What the teacher's lesson was about (a king, Ashoka) - the classroom Jahnavi listens at the door of, so the school concept rather than 28243 Jahnavi.
Crossword clue for 'yacht' - a boat with sails, rhymes with cot. Water-transport vocabulary from the coastal setting, alongside catamaran; not 28251, whose words are sound words.
Asks how the spider's journey shows anyone can be a source of inspiration - the poem's argument, in which the spider's example instructs the king. Not 28255, which is the bare moral about failure.
Matches 'to try very hard to achieve something' to endeavour, toil, strive, brace - exactly the poem's striving vocabulary, not a sound word (28251).
Why the poet describes every action of the spider in such detail and what that shows about his attitude - a question about how the poem builds its case, not the moral itself.
What King Bruce did after being inspired: he braced his mind and tried once more. The failed attempt calling for another attempt is 28255, not the poem's craft (28252).
What the gossips tell of King Bruce's final attempt - 'that time he did not fail'. The try-again-after-failure outcome, not 28254 vocabulary.
The spider dropping with its silken filmy clue at the exact moment the King decided to give up - the pivot on which the poem turns a failure into an instruction.
Describe the spider's difficult path: long way to the ceiling dome, a delicate thread to tread, a road where its feet would tire. Imagery serving the poem's argument, not the word list in 28254.
Nine brave attempts and the slippery sprawl after each - repeated failure that does not end the effort, which is 28255 rather than the poem's construction (28252).
The King's initial judgement that 'that foolish thing will strive no more to climb' - the mistaken reading the poem sets up in order to overturn it.
How the spider finally reached its cobweb home, steadily inch by inch with a bold little run at the last pinch - the demonstration that a failed attempt calls for another.
King Bruce's realisation, 'He conquered, and why shouldn't I?' - the poem's message about failure, applied to himself.
How King Bruce's attitude transformed after the spider's perseverance - the change the poem's argument is built to produce, so 28252 rather than the moral stated bare (28255).
What King Bruce was trying to do - a great deed to make his people glad. The first failure the poem starts from.
What suddenly appeared as the King was thinking: a spider. The turn in the poem's argument, not the moral (28255).
What the spider hung from - 'a silken, filmy clue'. Narrative detail inside the poem's argument; not 28254, which is the striving/despair word list.
Where the spider was trying to go - its cobweb home on the ceiling. The goal the repeated attempts are aimed at in the poem's argument.
How many attempts the spider made (nine) - the count of failures that still did not end the effort.
What happened after each climb: it fell down and got dizzy. Failure repeated and survived, which is 28255.
What the King thought of the spider after its failed attempts - foolish, and about to give up. The judgement the poem overturns.
Did the spider stop trying after falling? No. This is the poem's message in its plainest form.
How the spider finally reached home - by climbing slowly without falling, after the falls. The second attempt succeeding.
What King Bruce shouted when the spider succeeded - 'Bravo, bravo!'. The King's response is the hinge of the poem's argument.
What lesson King Bruce learned: to keep trying and never give up. The explicit moral, so 28255 and not 28252.
Where the spider was climbing to - the ceiling dome. Narrative detail of the climb the poem argues from.
What feeling the spider showed by trying repeatedly: courage and hope rather than despair - 28255 states exactly that contrast.
Assertion-reason on the King feeling like giving up because he had tried many times without success - the first failure the poem begins from.
Assertion-reason on the spider being dizzy and faint and on the delicate thread - tests how the poem's details relate, not the moral.
Assertion-reason: the King despaired at his own failures, but the reason offered (the spider's failures made him give up) is false. Tests the direction of the poem's argument.
Assertion-reason on the 'foolish thing' continuing to climb and the King being inspired to try again - the failure-is-not-the-end message.
What mood King Bruce was in at the beginning - a lonely mood to think. The poem's opening position before the instruction.
What the King was trying to do for his people - a great deed to make them glad. The undertaking that had first failed.
